en: *Samvarodayatantra*, Chapter 12: The Chapter on the Instruction Concerning the Rosary for Mantra Recitation Listen correctly, O Lord of Vajras, to the characteristics of the rosary (*akṣasūtra*), by which, through the correct procedure, [results] are accomplished; of this there is no doubt. (12.1) Gold, silver, copper, crystal, conch-shell, and so forth—these one should employ for the rites of pacification (*śānti*) and enrichment (*puṣṭi*), using beads (*gulikā*) of such materials. (12.2) One hundred and eight beads are recommended for the rite of enrichment. For the sake of a king, the mantra-practitioner (*mantrī*) should recite [the mantra] for the sake of prosperity, wealth, happiness, and festivals. (12.3) Saffron and other fragrant substances, coral, red sandalwood, and seeds—these are always used for fifty beads in the applications of subjugation (*vaśya*) and attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*). (12.4) Rudrākṣa seeds, *ariṣṭa* seeds, human bone, and likewise the bones of camels, donkeys, and buffaloes are used for the rite of sorcery (*abhicāra*), muteness, and paralyzing. (12.5) For killing, expulsion, causing hatred, and the suppression of enemies, one should fashion the rosary according to the specific requirements of the ritual. (12.6) The hair of a donkey or a camel mixed with the wing-feathers of a crow, knotted together with that thread, is used for the rites of paralyzing and expulsion. (12.7) The hair of a horse or a ram, mixed with the hair of a dog, and a thread made from the hair of a corpse from a cremation ground—such a thread is praised for application in cruel rites. For auspicious rites, one should knot the thread spun by a maiden. (12.8–12.9) In the rite of pacification, one should place the thumb; in the rite of enrichment, always the middle finger; the ring finger is said to be for subjugation; and the little finger is for sorcery. (12.10) The thumb should be employed in all rites as the form of the deity. One should regard every bead as being of the very nature of the *dharmadhātu*. (12.11) The rosary is distinguished by the state of meditative concentration during recitation. In the Kṛta age, one should recite once; in the Tretā age, one should recite twice. (12.12) In the Dvāpara age, it is taught that it should be triple; in the Kali age, the recitation is fourfold. One should recite the mantra continuously, for the four [ages] are the forms of the mantra. (12.13) This recitation consists of vocal utterance and the collection of the rosary and so forth. It has the nature of the manifestation and withdrawal of the form of the deity’s speech, which is perceived. (12.14) Having contemplated the coming and going [of the breath] through the reality of the symbolic mantra, one reaches the ultimate *tathatā*, which is free from the three extremes. The characteristic and the rule for these mantra-recitations are now declared. (12.15) Thus ends the twelfth chapter, the Chapter on the Instruction Concerning the Rosary for Mantra Recitation.
